The [[1952 Winter Olympics]], officially known as the ''VI Olympic Winter Games'', took place in [[Oslo]], [[Norway]], from 14 to 25&nbsp;February&nbsp;1952.  A total of 694 athletes representing 30 [[National Olympic Committees]] (NOCs) participated in the Games, taking part in 22 events from 6 [[Olympic sports|sports]].<ref name=oslo>{{cite web|title=Oslo 1952|publisher=International Olympic Committee|url=http://www.olympic.org/oslo-1952-winter-olympics|access-date=27 April 2011|archive-date=25 December 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181225173303/https://www.olympic.org/oslo-1952|url-status=live}}</ref>

From the thirteen NOCs that collected at least one medal, eight secured at least one gold. Ten NOCs won more than one medal, and among these, [[Norway at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Norway]] was the most successful with sixteen medals, including seven golds. The [[United States at the 1952 Winter Olympics|United States]] (eleven medals, four golds) and [[Finland at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Finland]] (nine medals, three golds) finished second and third in the medal table, respectively.<ref name="sr1952">{{cite Sports-Reference|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/|title=1952 Oslo Winter Games|access-date=7 July 2011| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110722211912/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/| archive-date= 22 July 2011 | url-status= dead}}</ref>

Norway's [[Hjalmar Andersen]] and [[Germany at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Germany]]'s [[Mirl Buchner]] were the top [[list of 1952 Winter Olympics medal winners|medal winners]], with three medals each.<ref name="sr1952"/> The [[Netherlands at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Netherlands]] got its first Winter Olympics medals, when [[Kees Broekman]] and [[Wim van der Voort]] won three silver medals between them in [[speed skating at the 1952 Winter Olympics|speed skating]].<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/NED/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417093436/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/NED/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|title=Netherlands|access-date=7 July 2011}}</ref> [[Portugal at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Portugal]] and [[New Zealand at the 1952 Winter Olympics|New Zealand]] made their Winter Olympic Games debuts in Oslo, but neither nation won a medal.<ref name="oslo"/>

==Highlights==
{{see also|1952 Winter Olympics}}
[[File:Bob 1952 vorne.jpg|thumb|right|alt=metallic sled with the word Deutschland 1 emblazoned on the front|The gold medal-winning four-man bobsleigh from Germany]]
Oslo was the first Scandinavian city to host a Winter Olympics.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Historical Dictionary of the Modern Olympic Movement|last1=Findling|first1=John E.|last2=Pelle|first2=Kimberly D.|publisher=Greenwood Publishing Group|location=Westport, United States|year=1996|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vj5-Srq3ki4C&q=oslo+winter+olympics+pelle&pg=PA252|isbn=0-313-28477-6| access-date= 13 September 2011 }}</ref> Athletes from the host nation won more medals than any other nation.  Truck driver Hjalmar Andersen won three out of the four speed skating events, and [[Simon Slåttvik]] and [[Sverre Stenersen]] won gold and bronze in [[Nordic combined]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Speed Skating History|publisher=National Speed Skating Museum|format=Word document|url=http://www.nationalspeedskatingmuseum.org/Docs/Handbook-History/SSHIST.doc|access-date=31 August 2010|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110727112640/http://www.nationalspeedskatingmuseum.org/Docs/Handbook-History/SSHIST.doc|archive-date=27 July 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Nordic Combined at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/NCO/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417043439/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/NCO/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=31 August 2010}}</ref>  Ski jumpers [[Arnfinn Bergmann]] and [[Torbjørn Falkanger]] placed first and second, and only [[Sweden at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Swedish]] jumper [[Karl Holmström]] prevented a Norwegian sweep.<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Ski Jumping at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/SKJ/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417043501/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/SKJ/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=31 August 2010}}</ref>

After a 16-year hiatus from Olympic competition [[Germany at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Germany]] made a triumphant return, winning seven medals and three golds.<ref name=oslosr>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=1952 Oslo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/|access-date=26 August 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100829092629/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/| archive-date= 29 August 2010 | url-status= dead}}</ref>  They won gold medals in both two- and four-man bobsleigh events.  The results for both events were identical with the United States and [[Switzerland at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Switzerland]] taking silver and bronze.<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Bobsleigh at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/BOB/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417043459/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/BOB/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=31 August 2010}}</ref>  The other gold medal for Germany went to the husband and wife figure skating pair of [[Paul Falk (figure skater)|Paul]] and [[Ria Falk]], who won the mixed pairs competition.<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Germany Figure Skating at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/GER/winter/1952/FSK/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417080935/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/GER/winter/1952/FSK/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=31 August 2010}}</ref>  [[Mirl Buchner]] of Germany was the only other triple medalist when she won three medals in alpine skiing, placing second in the downhill and third in the slalom and giant slalom.<ref>{{cite web|title=1952 Winter Olympics |publisher=Database Olympics |url=http://www.databaseolympics.com/games/gamessport.htm?g=32&sp=ALP |access-date=7 July 2011 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110816013340/http://www.databaseolympics.com/games/gamessport.htm?g=32&sp=ALP |archive-date=16 August 2011 }}</ref>

[[Wim van der Voort]] from the [[Netherlands at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Netherlands]] placed second in the 1,500&nbsp;meter speed skating events and his countryman [[Kees Broekman]] placed second in the 5,000 and 10,000-meter races.  These were the first-ever Dutch medals at the Winter Olympics.<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Speed Skating at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/SSK/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417043455/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/SSK/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=31 August 2010}}</ref>  [[Great Britain at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Great Britain's]] lone medal was won by [[Jeannette Altwegg]], who became only the second British woman to win the ladies' figure skating competition.<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Great Britain Figure Skating Women's Singles Results|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/GBR/winter/FSK/womens-singles.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417231805/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/countries/GBR/winter/FSK/womens-singles.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=7 July 2011}}</ref>  [[Dick Button]] and [[James Grogan]] of the United States won gold and bronze in the men's figure skating event.<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Figure Skating at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games-Men's Singles|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/FSK/mens-singles.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417201147/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/FSK/mens-singles.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=31 August 2010}}</ref> Button became the first figure skater to land a triple jump in competition when he performed the [[Loop jump|triple loop]] in the men's free skate program.<ref>{{cite web|title=Oslo 1952 Overview|publisher=ESPN|url=http://espn.go.com/olympics/winter/history/_/year/1952|access-date=31 August 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100731001212/http://espn.go.com/olympics/winter/history/_/year/1952| archive-date= 31 July 2010 | url-status= dead}}</ref>

Finnish athletes won nine medals and three golds at the Games.  They dominated the cross-country events, winning eight out of a possible twelve medals.<ref name=srcc>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Cross Country Skiing at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/CCS/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417043453/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/CCS/|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|access-date=31 August 2010}}</ref>  A women's race was added to the cross-country program for the first time and Finnish skiers [[Lydia Wideman]], [[Mirja Hietamies]] and [[Siiri Rantanen]] swept the event.<ref name=srcc/>  [[Veikko Hakulinen]] won the 50-kilometer men's race to begin an Olympic career that would culminate in seven medals, three of them gold.<ref>{{Cite book|title=The Winter Olympics|last=Judd|first=Ron C.|publisher=The Mountaineers Books|location=Seattle, United States|year=2008|isbn=978-1-59485-063-9|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Hc2dCHfyh0AC| access-date= 7 July 2011 }}</ref>

The ice hockey tournament was won by [[Canada at the 1952 Winter Olympics|Canada]]. Their gold medal game against the United States ended in a tie, and  International rules at the time did not allow for overtime, so the gold medal was awarded to Canada on goal differential.<ref name=srhockey>{{cite Sports-Reference|title=Ice Hockey at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/ICH/|access-date=31 August 2010| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20100829090228/http://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/ICH/| archive-date= 29 August 2010 | url-status= dead}}</ref>  Canada had won all but one Olympic hockey tournament thus far, but in 1956 the Soviet team entered the competition and ended Canadian dominance.<ref>{{cite web|title=1952 – Winter Olympics VI (Oslo, Norway)|publisher=The Sports Network (TSN)|url=https://www.tsn.ca/olympics/feature/?fid=10270|access-date=2 May 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110604053103/http://www.tsn.ca/olympics/feature/?fid=10270|archive-date=4 June 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Medal table==
{{see also|Olympic medal table}}
The medal table is based on information provided by the [[International Olympic Committee]] (IOC) and is consistent with IOC convention in its published medal tables. The table uses the [[Olympic medal table]] sorting method. By default, the table is ordered by the number of gold medals the athletes from a nation have won, where a nation is an entity represented by a [[National Olympic Committee]] (NOC). The number of silver medals is taken into consideration next, and then the number of bronze medals.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ostlere |first1=Lawrence |date=11 August 2024 |title=Olympic medal table: USA beat China to top spot at Paris 2024 |url=https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/olympics/olympics-2024-medal-table-count-paris-b2580716.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240812015233/https://www.independent.co.uk/sport/olympics/olympics-2024-medal-table-count-paris-b2594580.html |archive-date=12 August 2024 |access-date=12 August 2024 |work=[[The Independent]] |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last1=Araton |first1=Harvey |date=18 August 2008 |title=A Medal Count That Adds Up To Little |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/19/sports/olympics/19araton.html |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230321004238/https://www.nytimes.com/2008/08/19/sports/olympics/19araton.html |archive-date=21 March 2023 |access-date=25 July 2024 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> If teams are still tied, equal ranking is given and they are listed alphabetically by their [[List of IOC country codes|IOC country code]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Cons |first1=Roddy |date=10 August 2024 |title=What happens if two countries are tied in the Olympic medal table? Tiebreaker rules explained |url=https://en.as.com/olympic_games/what-happens-if-two-countries-are-tied-in-the-olympic-medal-table-tiebreaker-rules-explained-n/ |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240811152350/https://en.as.com/olympic_games/what-happens-if-two-countries-are-tied-in-the-olympic-medal-table-tiebreaker-rules-explained-n/ |archive-date=August 11, 2024 |access-date=11 August 2024 |work=[[Diario AS]] |language=en-us}}</ref>

There was a tie for third place in the [[Speed skating at the 1952 Winter Olympics – Men's 500 metres|men's 500-metre]] event in speed skating, therefore two bronze medals were awarded.<ref>{{cite Sports-Reference|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/SSK/mens-500-metres.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200417192326/https://www.sports-reference.com/olympics/winter/1952/SSK/mens-500-metres.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=17 April 2020|title=Speed Skating at the 1952 Oslo Winter Games: Men's 500 metres|access-date=29 December 2010}}</ref>
